props.name: Cu2/Cu3 preserve symmetric Cu-Cu configurations and sustain C2+ formation

evidence.quote: Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that catalysts with insufficient steric constraint undergo asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, leading to heterogeneous *CO adsorption behavior and enhanced C1 pathways. In contrast, sterically stabilized catalysts preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain favorable *CO–*CO coupling toward C2 + formation. These findings demonstrate that geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions, rather than the initial structure alone, governs catalytic selectivity in CO2 electroreduction and highlights the importance of operando characterization for identifying active-state structures. KEYWORDS: eCO2RR, secondary coordination sphere, local environment, operando spectroscopy, Cu–Cu distance ■INTRODUCTION Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) offers a promising strategy for converting CO2 into value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable electricity.1–3 Although recent advances in electrolyzer engineering have enabled CO2RR at industrially relevant current density and selectivity,4,5 achieving highly selective multi-carbon (C2 +) production remains a major challenge due to the complex reaction pathways involved in C–C coupling6 and the associated separation cost of mixed products.7,8 The formation of multi-carbon products during eCO2RR involves complex proton-coupled multi-electron transfer pathways and kinetically demanding C–C coupling processes, often resulting in broad product distributions and reduced selectivity.9,10 Consequently, catalyst design strategies capable of regulating intermediate adsorption and coupling behavior are critically important for improving multi-carbon selectivity.11,12 In ligand-coordinated Cu catalysts, the formation of multicarbon products has been strongly associated with the presence of adjacent Cu centers.13,14 Cu is uniquely capable among monometallic catalysts of producing substantial multi-carbon products by eCO2RR.3,15 However, isolated Cu single sites predominantly produce single-carbon products under reaction conditions,16–20 whereas paired Cu centers have been associated with enhanced C2 + formation.21 Previous studies further revealed that replacing one Cu center with heteroatoms significantly alters intermediate adsorption energetics and suppresses multi-carbon pathways,22 suggesting that adjacent Cu centers play a critical role in C–C coupling during eCO2RR. Motivated by this mechanistic hypothesis, increasing efforts have focused on engineering the microenvironment of the Cu active site,23–25 especially the Cu–Cu spacing in multinuclear Cu catalysts. Recent studies have reported dual- and multinuclear Cu systems with Cu–Cu distances ranging from 2.54 to 3.52 Å, including halogen-bridged dual-copper catalysts,14,26,27 carbon supported molecular catalysts,28 metal–organic polymers,29 and triazole-bridged MOF structures,30 all demonstrating appreciable C2 + selectivity under eCO2RR conditions. The importance of Cu–Cu spacing has been attributed to its influence on the adsorption geometry and coupling probability of adjacent *CO intermediates, which are widely considered key steps toward multi-carbon formation.10,31,32 Accordingly, considerable efforts have been devoted to rigidly controlling Received: June 4, 2026 Revised: August 7, 2026 Accepted: August 7, 2026 www.acsami.org Research Article This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.6c11350 ACS Appl. Despite the growing emphasis on Cu–Cu spacing engineering, the structural evolution of dual-Cu sites under operating conditions remains poorly understood. Previous studies have provided valuable structural insights through pre- and postreaction characterization; however, direct operando observations of Cu–Cu dynamics during eCO2RR remain scarce. (Figure 1a) Given the highly dynamic nature of electrocatalytic interfaces under bias,33,34 static structural assignments obtained before or after reaction may not fully capture the realistic catalytic configurations responsible for intermediate coupling during eCO2RR. Such configurational flexibility has been proposed to provide diverse adsorption geometries for adjacent *CO intermediates, potentially facilitating C–C coupling toward multi-carbon products.26,35 However, without direct experimental evidence confirming reversible Cu–Cu stretching under reaction conditions, its relationship to catalytic selectivity has yet to be experimentally established. Here, we investigate how ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution and selectivity of a series of trinuclear Cu catalysts during eCO2RR. By combining operando X-ray absorption and Raman spectroscopies,36,37 we track changes in Cu–Cu coordination and *CO adsorption under working conditions. We find that catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu–Cu configuration and favor C2 + formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity. These results identify active-state geometric persistence, rather than the initial coordination structure alone, as a key design parameter for eCO2RR targeting multi-carbon products.36,37 ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Materials All reagents and chemicals were commercially available and used without further purification. The corresponding yellow to green dicopper(I) MOFs in the π–π stacking framework are air- and moisture-stable in the solid state. The synthesized electrocatalysts were air-sprayed onto a gas-diffusion electrode as the working electrode. Cu1 is reported to be highly active toward CO2 reduction producing ethylene.30 Cu2 and Cu3 are also electroactive for eCO2RR but with higher selectivity toward multi-carbon products within the same potential range than Cu1 (Figure 1c,d). Figure 1c displays the C1 product profile of 3 electrocatalysts under alkaline eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE. Specifically, CH4 is the dominant product for Cu1, while Cu2 and Cu3 produce ethylene and ethanol as major products (Figure 1d). These results indicate that the structural features of Cu2 and Cu3 preferentially promote the C2 + dominant reaction pathway relative to C1. Although the structurally equivalent CuBtz30 catalyst was previously reported to exhibit high C2 + selectivity, Cu1 displays a C1-dominant product distribution under the conditions employed here. The two studies employed substantially different catalyst-layer configurations, which can alter the local reaction environment and thereby influence the working-state structure and product selectivity of Cu catalysts,42,43 as discussed in Note S1. This contrast further underscores that catalytic behavior cannot be inferred solely from the nominal pristine structure and highlights the importance of correlating product selectivity with the active-state structure observed under operating conditions. Figure 1e compares the partial current density for the C2 + product of 3 electrocatalysts. Cu3 possessed the highest partial current density peaking at –1.2 V vs. RHE, followed by Cu2 and Cu1. However, the ratio of multicarbon products over single carbon products is different among 3 electrocatalysts. This trend demonstrates that eCO2RR over Cu1 increasingly favors the C1-dominant pathway as the cathodic overpotential increases, compared to Cu2 and Cu3. We proceed to reveal the structural properties that might lead to the difference in selectivity. Characterization with powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Figure S1) confirmed that the structure is similar to that in previous work30 for Cu1. The XRD pattern of Cu2 shows diffraction features similar to those of Cu1. Compared with the PXRD pattern of Cu1, Cu3 exhibits shifts in several diffraction peaks, suggesting differences in the long-range crystallographic order. Because PXRD alone cannot establish whether the local Cu coordination motif is preserved, the local electronic and coordination structures were further examined later using X-ray absorption spectroscopy. The morphologies of the pristine Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 samples were examined by HR-SEM (Figure S2). Although these morphological differences may affect the electrochemically accessible surface area, product selectivity does not necessarily scale directly with the total accessible surface area. Therefore, the discussion below focuses primarily on the relationship between the distinct local coordination motifs identified and the observed selectivity trends, while recognizing that a contribution from particle morphology cannot be completely excluded. The Raman spectra of the pristine structures confirm the preservation of the triazole ligands after synthesis44 (Figure S3). N K-edge XANES spectra of Cu1 to Cu3 (Figure S4) exhibit nearly identical π* and σ* adsorption features, with no measurable shift in edge onset or variation in the peak position within experimental resolution (0.1 eV). Because N K-edge XAS is sensitive to unoccupied N 2pderived states that reflect metal–ligand orbital mixing and covalency,45 the preserved spectral features indicate comparable Cu–N electronic interactions across all three catalysts, excluding the modulation of the electronic structure as the origin of the divergent product distribution. Cu L-edge spectra display nearly identical white-line intensities and multiplet features for all catalysts (Figure S5), indicating comparable 2p– 3d transition and similar populations of the unoccupied Cu 3d state.46 The preserved spectral features are consistent with a predominantly Cu(I) electronic configuration in the pristine structures. No discernible shift in the L3 edge position is observed, further supporting electronic similarity among the three catalysts. Operando Raman spectroscopy was further employed to probe the interfacial behavior of adsorbed intermediates during eCO2RR (Figure 2). For Cu1, the bands at ∼2050 and 2080 cm–1 are assigned to the low- and high-frequency C≡O stretching modes of linearly adsorbed CO (*CO) on Cu, respectively, consistent with previous in situ and operando vibrational spectroscopic studies.37,47–49 The precise surface environments responsible for these bands may depend on the Cu surface structure, applied potential, and CO coverage. Accordingly, the observed frequency difference may reflect variations in the local Cu–CO coordination environment and Cuto-CO back-donation strength.50 In addition, operando Raman measurements have simultaneously distinguished surfaceadsorbed carbonate at approximately 1055 cm–1 from adsorbed CO at approximately 2080 cm–1, further supporting the assignment of the bands in the 2050–2080 cm–1 region to adsorbed CO rather than carbonate species.51,52 Accordingly, as shown in Figure 2a, the intensity of the *CO2080 band becomes more prominent at more cathodic potential at –1.2 V. Upon reversing the potential sweep, the *CO2050 band is dominant again. Finally, the *CO settled at 2070 cm–1 when back to –0.7 V. The persistence of the *CO signal during the reverse sweep indicates that an appreciable population of surface-bound *CO remains under these conditions, suggesting a relatively stable Cu–*CO interaction and/or slow interfacial CO removal.37 The persistent accumulation of surface-bound *CO may favor subsequent hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products over efficient *CO–*CO coupling. Despite the similar geometric and electronic structures of the three catalysts, the *CO adsorption behavior on Cu2 and Cu3 differs markedly from that on Cu1 (Figure 2b,c). When cathodic potential increases, the *CO in Cu2 shows up at –1.0 V in the range of 2020–2080 cm–1 (Figure 2b). Such substantial spectral broadening implies a heterogeneous and dynamically fluctuating interfacial environment, where *CO experiences a continuum of Cu binding geometries and interaction strengths.37,53,54 When the driving potential further increases to –1.2 V and comes back to –1.1 V vs RHE, the Figure 2. The operando XANES remains the same for Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 throughout the applied potentials with no resolvable shifts in the edge fingerprint within the experimental resolution (Figure S7). The observation indicates that the predominantly Cu(I) oxidation state is preserved under the applied potential, which has been proposed to favor *CO–*CO coupling.62 Within the sensitivity of the present measurements, no substantial ensemble-averaged electronic restructuring is detected. Subtle charge redistribution, adsorbate-induced changes in metal–ligand covalency, transient electronic states, or changes confined to a minority population of the active site may not be resolved by XANES. Accordingly, Cu–Cu geometry evolution represents the dominant changes detected under the relevant operando conditions. Figure 3c–e shows the evolution of coordination shells for Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3, respectively, during alkaline CO2 electroreduction. From Figure 3c, Fourier-transform EXAFS spectra (k3-weighted, 2.5 to 10.5 Å–1) reveal progressive splitting of the Cu–Cu scattering feature centered at ∼3.5 Å under increasing cathodic bias from –0.7 to –0.9 V. Further EXAFS fitting yields a contraction of one Cu–Cu distance from 3.68 ± 0.02 to 3.54 ± 0.01 Å, accompanied by expansion of a second path to 4.05 ± 0.01 Å from –0.7 to –1.2 V vs RHE. The prominent peak of Cu–N2 also shows distortion alongside, in resonance to the stretch of the coordination structure around the copper centers, which supports the suspected asymmetric Cu–Cu spacing. Conversely, the Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 remains unchanged at all cathodic potentials, as shown in Figure 3d,e, respectively. Time-dependent operando XAS further confirms that Cu1 retains a distorted local coordination framework without complete collapse during 3 h of continuous eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE (Figure S32). We propose that the ligand-derived steric confinement (Figure 5) stabilizes the Cu–Cu configuration in Cu2 and Cu3 by restricting Cu-site displacement and suppressing pronounced asymmetric distortion. This structural persistence could preserve the integrity of their local coordination environments under applied bias, thereby maintaining welldefined sites for the adsorption and conversion of eCO2RR intermediates. Specifically, the onset potential of Cu–Cu splitting at –0.9 V corresponds to the onset potential when two distinct *CO bands (2050 and 2080 cm–1) emerged with Cu1. The shortened Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuS) may induce stronger confinement of adsorbed *CO species, potentially altering their adsorption configuration from terminal-like to more bridge-like coordination. In contrast, the elongated Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuL) likely increases the separation between neighboring adsorbates, thereby reducing the probability of effective *CO–*CO coupling. Such asymmetric Cu–Cu environments may therefore favor sequential hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products, consistent with the enhanced CH4 selectivity observed for Cu1 in Figure 1c. In contrast, the preserved Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 under cathodic bias may better maintain favorable geometric configurations for *CO–*CO coupling. Accordingly, the preservation of symmetric Cu–Cu spacing provides a stable geometric environment favorable for sustained C–C coupling. The introduction of steric hindrance through ligand modification on either benzoic ring or azole nitrogen therefore plays a critical role in preserving the intrinsic Cu–Cu spacing as it is under bias. The absence of detectable changes in the electronic structure of copper under bias further supports the conclusion that geometric stability, rather than electronic modulation, governs the divergent reaction pathways. With that being said, localized rearrangements cannot be completely excluded. Local interfacial electric fields may also influence C–C coupling by stabilizing polar intermediates such as *OCCO through field–dipole interactions.70,71 Taken together, these results establish Cu–Cu geometric persistence as the dominant structural descriptor governing C2 + selectivity in this catalyst series, while other potential microenvironmental factors arising at the catalyst–electrolyte interface may also contribute. The performance of Cu1–Cu3 was compared with that of representative molecular Cu-based catalysts containing adjacent Cu sites (Table S4). Cu2 and Cu3 exhibit C2 + performance within the reported range; however, no simple relationship between Cu–Cu distance and C2 + selectivity is evident. Notably, operando Cu–Cu structures are unavailable for most reported catalysts, limiting direct structure–activity comparisons. To sum up, these findings highlight the necessity of operando characterization to capture the dynamic structural evolution under bias, even for catalysts with structurally welldefined molecular motifs that appear preserved after catalysis by ex situ characterization. ■CONCLUSIONS This work demonstrates that the divergent catalytic behaviors of dual-Cu-site catalysts originate from their distinct active-state structural evolution under reaction conditions rather than differences in their initial coordination structures or electronic states. Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that Cu1 undergoes asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, resulting in heterogeneous *CO binding environments that favor C1 pathways, whereas the sterically stabilized Cu2 and Cu3 preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain C–C coupling toward enhanced C2 + formation. These findings establish geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions as a critical parameter for multicarbon CO2 electroreduction.

These results identify active-state geometric persistence, rather than the initial coordination structure alone, as a key design parameter for eCO2RR targeting multi-carbon products.

props.name: Ligand-derived steric confinement stabilizes the Cu-Cu configuration in Cu2/Cu3

evidence.quote: We propose that the ligand-derived steric confinement (Figure 5) stabilizes the Cu–Cu configuration in Cu2 and Cu3 by restricting Cu-site displacement and suppressing pronounced asymmetric distortion.

This structural persistence could preserve the integrity of their local coordination environments under applied bias, thereby maintaining welldefined sites for the adsorption and conversion of eCO2RR intermediates.

props.name: Ligand-imposed steric rigidity governs active-state evolution and C2+ selectivity

evidence.quote: Here, we investigate how ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution and selectivity of a series of trinuclear Cu catalysts during eCO2RR. By combining operando X-ray absorption and Raman spectroscopies,36,37 we track changes in Cu–Cu coordination and *CO adsorption under working conditions.

We find that catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu–Cu configuration and favor C2 + formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity.

props.statement: Ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution of trinuclear Cu motifs during eCO2RR: catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu-Cu configuration and favor C2+ formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity.

props.name: Cu1 working state: asymmetric Cu-Cu distortion

onset.text_value: Cu-Cu splitting after -0.9 V vs RHE

persists.text_value: retained without complete collapse during 3 h at -1.2 V vs RHE

evidence.quote: This inconsistency in the changes of copper distances leads to the structure of asymmetric Cu–Cu spacing, as visualized in Figure 3a. The prominent peak of Cu–N2 also shows distortion alongside, in resonance to the stretch of the coordination structure around the copper centers, which supports the suspected asymmetric Cu–Cu spacing. Conversely, the Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 remains unchanged at all cathodic potentials, as shown in Figure 3d,e, respectively.
Cu1 exhibits Cu–Cu splitting after –0.9 V vs RHE, resulting
in the emergence of shortened (Cu–CuS) and elongated (Cu–CuL) Cu–Cu spacings, while the dual copper spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 remains unchanged.
WT-EXAFS maps of Cu1 in the (a) pristine state and (b) under –1.2 V vs RHE in 1 M KOH.

props.morphology: under cathodic bias >= -0.9 V vs RHE the symmetric ~3.5 A Cu-Cu feature of Cu1 splits into a shortened (Cu-CuS, ~3.54 A at -1.2 V vs RHE) and an elongated (Cu-CuL, ~4.05 A) Cu-Cu spacing, i.e. asymmetric Cu-Cu coordination

Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that catalysts with insufficient steric constraint undergo asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, leading to heterogeneous *CO adsorption behavior and enhanced C1 pathways. In contrast, sterically stabilized catalysts preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain favorable *CO–*CO coupling toward C2 + formation. These findings demonstrate that geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions, rather than the initial structure alone, governs catalytic selectivity in CO2 electroreduction and highlights the importance of operando characterization for identifying active-state structures. KEYWORDS: eCO2RR, secondary coordination sphere, local environment, operando spectroscopy, Cu–Cu distance ■INTRODUCTION Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) offers a promising strategy for converting CO2 into value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable electricity.1–3 Although recent advances in electrolyzer engineering have enabled CO2RR at industrially relevant current density and selectivity,4,5 achieving highly selective multi-carbon (C2 +) production remains a major challenge due to the complex reaction pathways involved in C–C coupling6 and the associated separation cost of mixed products.7,8 The formation of multi-carbon products during eCO2RR involves complex proton-coupled multi-electron transfer pathways and kinetically demanding C–C coupling processes, often resulting in broad product distributions and reduced selectivity.9,10 Consequently, catalyst design strategies capable of regulating intermediate adsorption and coupling behavior are critically important for improving multi-carbon selectivity.11,12 In ligand-coordinated Cu catalysts, the formation of multicarbon products has been strongly associated with the presence of adjacent Cu centers.13,14 Cu is uniquely capable among monometallic catalysts of producing substantial multi-carbon products by eCO2RR.3,15 However, isolated Cu single sites predominantly produce single-carbon products under reaction conditions,16–20 whereas paired Cu centers have been associated with enhanced C2 + formation.21 Previous studies further revealed that replacing one Cu center with heteroatoms significantly alters intermediate adsorption energetics and suppresses multi-carbon pathways,22 suggesting that adjacent Cu centers play a critical role in C–C coupling during eCO2RR. Motivated by this mechanistic hypothesis, increasing efforts have focused on engineering the microenvironment of the Cu active site,23–25 especially the Cu–Cu spacing in multinuclear Cu catalysts. Recent studies have reported dual- and multinuclear Cu systems with Cu–Cu distances ranging from 2.54 to 3.52 Å, including halogen-bridged dual-copper catalysts,14,26,27 carbon supported molecular catalysts,28 metal–organic polymers,29 and triazole-bridged MOF structures,30 all demonstrating appreciable C2 + selectivity under eCO2RR conditions. The importance of Cu–Cu spacing has been attributed to its influence on the adsorption geometry and coupling probability of adjacent *CO intermediates, which are widely considered key steps toward multi-carbon formation.10,31,32 Accordingly, considerable efforts have been devoted to rigidly controlling Received: June 4, 2026 Revised: August 7, 2026 Accepted: August 7, 2026 www.acsami.org Research Article This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.6c11350 ACS Appl. Despite the growing emphasis on Cu–Cu spacing engineering, the structural evolution of dual-Cu sites under operating conditions remains poorly understood. Previous studies have provided valuable structural insights through pre- and postreaction characterization; however, direct operando observations of Cu–Cu dynamics during eCO2RR remain scarce. (Figure 1a) Given the highly dynamic nature of electrocatalytic interfaces under bias,33,34 static structural assignments obtained before or after reaction may not fully capture the realistic catalytic configurations responsible for intermediate coupling during eCO2RR. Such configurational flexibility has been proposed to provide diverse adsorption geometries for adjacent *CO intermediates, potentially facilitating C–C coupling toward multi-carbon products.26,35 However, without direct experimental evidence confirming reversible Cu–Cu stretching under reaction conditions, its relationship to catalytic selectivity has yet to be experimentally established. Here, we investigate how ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution and selectivity of a series of trinuclear Cu catalysts during eCO2RR. By combining operando X-ray absorption and Raman spectroscopies,36,37 we track changes in Cu–Cu coordination and *CO adsorption under working conditions. We find that catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu–Cu configuration and favor C2 + formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity. These results identify active-state geometric persistence, rather than the initial coordination structure alone, as a key design parameter for eCO2RR targeting multi-carbon products.36,37 ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Materials All reagents and chemicals were commercially available and used without further purification. The corresponding yellow to green dicopper(I) MOFs in the π–π stacking framework are air- and moisture-stable in the solid state. The synthesized electrocatalysts were air-sprayed onto a gas-diffusion electrode as the working electrode. Cu1 is reported to be highly active toward CO2 reduction producing ethylene.30 Cu2 and Cu3 are also electroactive for eCO2RR but with higher selectivity toward multi-carbon products within the same potential range than Cu1 (Figure 1c,d). Figure 1c displays the C1 product profile of 3 electrocatalysts under alkaline eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE. Specifically, CH4 is the dominant product for Cu1, while Cu2 and Cu3 produce ethylene and ethanol as major products (Figure 1d). These results indicate that the structural features of Cu2 and Cu3 preferentially promote the C2 + dominant reaction pathway relative to C1. Although the structurally equivalent CuBtz30 catalyst was previously reported to exhibit high C2 + selectivity, Cu1 displays a C1-dominant product distribution under the conditions employed here. The two studies employed substantially different catalyst-layer configurations, which can alter the local reaction environment and thereby influence the working-state structure and product selectivity of Cu catalysts,42,43 as discussed in Note S1. This contrast further underscores that catalytic behavior cannot be inferred solely from the nominal pristine structure and highlights the importance of correlating product selectivity with the active-state structure observed under operating conditions. Figure 1e compares the partial current density for the C2 + product of 3 electrocatalysts. Cu3 possessed the highest partial current density peaking at –1.2 V vs. RHE, followed by Cu2 and Cu1. However, the ratio of multicarbon products over single carbon products is different among 3 electrocatalysts. We proceed to reveal the structural properties that might lead to the difference in selectivity. Characterization with powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Figure S1) confirmed that the structure is similar to that in previous work30 for Cu1. The XRD pattern of Cu2 shows diffraction features similar to those of Cu1. Compared with the PXRD pattern of Cu1, Cu3 exhibits shifts in several diffraction peaks, suggesting differences in the long-range crystallographic order. Because PXRD alone cannot establish whether the local Cu coordination motif is preserved, the local electronic and coordination structures were further examined later using X-ray absorption spectroscopy. The morphologies of the pristine Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 samples were examined by HR-SEM (Figure S2). Although these morphological differences may affect the electrochemically accessible surface area, product selectivity does not necessarily scale directly with the total accessible surface area. Therefore, the discussion below focuses primarily on the relationship between the distinct local coordination motifs identified and the observed selectivity trends, while recognizing that a contribution from particle morphology cannot be completely excluded. The Raman spectra of the pristine structures confirm the preservation of the triazole ligands after synthesis44 (Figure S3). N K-edge XANES spectra of Cu1 to Cu3 (Figure S4) exhibit nearly identical π* and σ* adsorption features, with no measurable shift in edge onset or variation in the peak position within experimental resolution (0.1 eV). Because N K-edge XAS is sensitive to unoccupied N 2pderived states that reflect metal–ligand orbital mixing and covalency,45 the preserved spectral features indicate comparable Cu–N electronic interactions across all three catalysts, excluding the modulation of the electronic structure as the origin of the divergent product distribution. Cu L-edge spectra display nearly identical white-line intensities and multiplet features for all catalysts (Figure S5), indicating comparable 2p– 3d transition and similar populations of the unoccupied Cu 3d state.46 The preserved spectral features are consistent with a predominantly Cu(I) electronic configuration in the pristine structures. No discernible shift in the L3 edge position is observed, further supporting electronic similarity among the three catalysts. Operando Raman spectroscopy was further employed to probe the interfacial behavior of adsorbed intermediates during eCO2RR (Figure 2). For Cu1, the bands at ∼2050 and 2080 cm–1 are assigned to the low- and high-frequency C≡O stretching modes of linearly adsorbed CO (*CO) on Cu, respectively, consistent with previous in situ and operando vibrational spectroscopic studies.37,47–49 The precise surface environments responsible for these bands may depend on the Cu surface structure, applied potential, and CO coverage. Accordingly, the observed frequency difference may reflect variations in the local Cu–CO coordination environment and Cuto-CO back-donation strength.50 In addition, operando Raman measurements have simultaneously distinguished surfaceadsorbed carbonate at approximately 1055 cm–1 from adsorbed CO at approximately 2080 cm–1, further supporting the assignment of the bands in the 2050–2080 cm–1 region to adsorbed CO rather than carbonate species.51,52 Accordingly, as shown in Figure 2a, the intensity of the *CO2080 band becomes more prominent at more cathodic potential at –1.2 V. Upon reversing the potential sweep, the *CO2050 band is dominant again. Finally, the *CO settled at 2070 cm–1 when back to –0.7 V. The persistence of the *CO signal during the reverse sweep indicates that an appreciable population of surface-bound *CO remains under these conditions, suggesting a relatively stable Cu–*CO interaction and/or slow interfacial CO removal.37 The persistent accumulation of surface-bound *CO may favor subsequent hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products over efficient *CO–*CO coupling. Despite the similar geometric and electronic structures of the three catalysts, the *CO adsorption behavior on Cu2 and Cu3 differs markedly from that on Cu1 (Figure 2b,c). When cathodic potential increases, the *CO in Cu2 shows up at –1.0 V in the range of 2020–2080 cm–1 (Figure 2b). Figure 3c–e shows the evolution of coordination shells for Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3, respectively, during alkaline CO2 electroreduction. From Figure 3c, Fourier-transform EXAFS spectra (k3-weighted, 2.5 to 10.5 Å–1) reveal progressive splitting of the Cu–Cu scattering feature centered at ∼3.5 Å under increasing cathodic bias from –0.7 to –0.9 V. This evolution indicates the emergence of asymmetric Cu– Cu coordination. Further EXAFS fitting yields a contraction of one Cu–Cu distance from 3.68 ± 0.02 to 3.54 ± 0.01 Å, accompanied by expansion of a second path to 4.05 ± 0.01 Å from –0.7 to –1.2 V vs RHE. The prominent peak of Cu–N2 also shows distortion alongside, in resonance to the stretch of the coordination structure around the copper centers, which supports the suspected asymmetric Cu–Cu spacing. Conversely, the Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 remains unchanged at all cathodic potentials, as shown in Figure 3d,e, respectively. To verify that the newly emerged scattering features in Cu1 under applied potential originate from the Cu–Cu scattering path rather than from light atoms in the coordination environment, such as C or N, wavelet-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (WT-EXAFS) analysis63 was performed. WT-EXAFS is particularly useful when different scattering paths appear at a similar apparent radial distance in Fourier-transform EXAFS because it provides simultaneous resolution in both R-space and k-space.64,65 Since the backscattering amplitude depends strongly on the atomic number of the scatterer, heavier atoms generally give stronger contributions at higher k values. Therefore, WT-EXAFS can help distinguish Cu scatterers from lighter C/N scatterers based on their different k-space intensity distribution.66 The WT-EXAFS contour plot of pristine Cu1 (Figure 4a) shows three major lobes assigned to Cu–N1, Cu–N2, and Cu– Cu scattering paths. These features appear at apparent distances of ∼1.7, 2.5, and 3.5 Å, with k-space maxima centered near 4.5, 4.5, and 6.5 Å–1, respectively. Under cathodic bias at –1.2 V vs RHE (Figure 4b), the Cu–Cu scattering feature broadens and shifts relative to the pristine state. Enlarged views of the Cu– Cu region (Figure 4c,d) reveal the emergence of additional high-k contribution centered near 8 Å–1 at an apparent distance of ∼3.2 Å, together with an expanded Cu–Cu feature extended toward ∼3.8 Å with a k-space maximum near 6.5 Å–1. The presence of these features in the high k region supports their assignment to Cu scattering paths rather than to light-atom contributions. These results therefore corroborate the operando FT-EXAFS observation that Cu1 undergoes asymmetric Cu– Cu distortion under cathodic bias. Time-dependent operando XAS further confirms that Cu1 retains a distorted local coordination framework without complete collapse during 3 h of continuous eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE (Figure S32). We propose that the ligand-derived steric confinement (Figure 5) stabilizes the Cu–Cu configuration in Cu2 and Cu3 by restricting Cu-site displacement and suppressing pronounced asymmetric distortion. This structural persistence could preserve the integrity of their local coordination environments under applied bias, thereby maintaining welldefined sites for the adsorption and conversion of eCO2RR intermediates. Specifically, the onset potential of Cu–Cu splitting at –0.9 V corresponds to the onset potential when two distinct *CO bands (2050 and 2080 cm–1) emerged with Cu1. The shortened Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuS) may induce stronger confinement of adsorbed *CO species, potentially altering their adsorption configuration from terminal-like to more bridge-like coordination. In contrast, the elongated Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuL) likely increases the separation between neighboring adsorbates, thereby reducing the probability of effective *CO–*CO coupling. Such asymmetric Cu–Cu environments may therefore favor sequential hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products, consistent with the enhanced CH4 selectivity observed for Cu1 in Figure 1c. In contrast, the preserved Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 under cathodic bias may better maintain favorable geometric configurations for *CO–*CO coupling. Accordingly, the preservation of symmetric Cu–Cu spacing provides a stable geometric environment favorable for sustained C–C coupling. The introduction of steric hindrance through ligand modification on either benzoic ring or azole nitrogen therefore plays a critical role in preserving the intrinsic Cu–Cu spacing as it is under bias. The absence of detectable changes in the electronic structure of copper under bias further supports the conclusion that geometric stability, rather than electronic modulation, governs the divergent reaction pathways. With that being said, localized rearrangements cannot be completely excluded. Local interfacial electric fields may also influence C–C coupling by stabilizing polar intermediates such as *OCCO through field–dipole interactions.70,71 Taken together, these results establish Cu–Cu geometric persistence as the dominant structural descriptor governing C2 + selectivity in this catalyst series, while other potential microenvironmental factors arising at the catalyst–electrolyte interface may also contribute. The performance of Cu1–Cu3 was compared with that of representative molecular Cu-based catalysts containing adjacent Cu sites (Table S4). Cu2 and Cu3 exhibit C2 + performance within the reported range; however, no simple relationship between Cu–Cu distance and C2 + selectivity is evident. Notably, operando Cu–Cu structures are unavailable for most reported catalysts, limiting direct structure–activity comparisons. To sum up, these findings highlight the necessity of operando characterization to capture the dynamic structural evolution under bias, even for catalysts with structurally welldefined molecular motifs that appear preserved after catalysis by ex situ characterization. ■CONCLUSIONS This work demonstrates that the divergent catalytic behaviors of dual-Cu-site catalysts originate from their distinct active-state structural evolution under reaction conditions rather than differences in their initial coordination structures or electronic states. Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that Cu1 undergoes asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, resulting in heterogeneous *CO binding environments that favor C1 pathways, whereas the sterically stabilized Cu2 and Cu3 preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain C–C coupling toward enhanced C2 + formation. These findings establish geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions as a critical parameter for multicarbon CO2 electroreduction.

Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that catalysts with insufficient steric constraint undergo asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, leading to heterogeneous *CO adsorption behavior and enhanced C1 pathways. In contrast, sterically stabilized catalysts preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain favorable *CO–*CO coupling toward C2 + formation. These findings demonstrate that geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions, rather than the initial structure alone, governs catalytic selectivity in CO2 electroreduction and highlights the importance of operando characterization for identifying active-state structures. KEYWORDS: eCO2RR, secondary coordination sphere, local environment, operando spectroscopy, Cu–Cu distance ■INTRODUCTION Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) offers a promising strategy for converting CO2 into value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable electricity.1–3 Although recent advances in electrolyzer engineering have enabled CO2RR at industrially relevant current density and selectivity,4,5 achieving highly selective multi-carbon (C2 +) production remains a major challenge due to the complex reaction pathways involved in C–C coupling6 and the associated separation cost of mixed products.7,8 The formation of multi-carbon products during eCO2RR involves complex proton-coupled multi-electron transfer pathways and kinetically demanding C–C coupling processes, often resulting in broad product distributions and reduced selectivity.9,10 Consequently, catalyst design strategies capable of regulating intermediate adsorption and coupling behavior are critically important for improving multi-carbon selectivity.11,12 In ligand-coordinated Cu catalysts, the formation of multicarbon products has been strongly associated with the presence of adjacent Cu centers.13,14 Cu is uniquely capable among monometallic catalysts of producing substantial multi-carbon products by eCO2RR.3,15 However, isolated Cu single sites predominantly produce single-carbon products under reaction conditions,16–20 whereas paired Cu centers have been associated with enhanced C2 + formation.21 Previous studies further revealed that replacing one Cu center with heteroatoms significantly alters intermediate adsorption energetics and suppresses multi-carbon pathways,22 suggesting that adjacent Cu centers play a critical role in C–C coupling during eCO2RR. Motivated by this mechanistic hypothesis, increasing efforts have focused on engineering the microenvironment of the Cu active site,23–25 especially the Cu–Cu spacing in multinuclear Cu catalysts. Recent studies have reported dual- and multinuclear Cu systems with Cu–Cu distances ranging from 2.54 to 3.52 Å, including halogen-bridged dual-copper catalysts,14,26,27 carbon supported molecular catalysts,28 metal–organic polymers,29 and triazole-bridged MOF structures,30 all demonstrating appreciable C2 + selectivity under eCO2RR conditions. Despite the growing emphasis on Cu–Cu spacing engineering, the structural evolution of dual-Cu sites under operating conditions remains poorly understood. Previous studies have provided valuable structural insights through pre- and postreaction characterization; however, direct operando observations of Cu–Cu dynamics during eCO2RR remain scarce. (Figure 1a) Given the highly dynamic nature of electrocatalytic interfaces under bias,33,34 static structural assignments obtained before or after reaction may not fully capture the realistic catalytic configurations responsible for intermediate coupling during eCO2RR. Such configurational flexibility has been proposed to provide diverse adsorption geometries for adjacent *CO intermediates, potentially facilitating C–C coupling toward multi-carbon products.26,35 However, without direct experimental evidence confirming reversible Cu–Cu stretching under reaction conditions, its relationship to catalytic selectivity has yet to be experimentally established. Here, we investigate how ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution and selectivity of a series of trinuclear Cu catalysts during eCO2RR. By combining operando X-ray absorption and Raman spectroscopies,36,37 we track changes in Cu–Cu coordination and *CO adsorption under working conditions. We find that catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu–Cu configuration and favor C2 + formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity. These results identify active-state geometric persistence, rather than the initial coordination structure alone, as a key design parameter for eCO2RR targeting multi-carbon products.36,37 ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Materials All reagents and chemicals were commercially available and used without further purification. The corresponding yellow to green dicopper(I) MOFs in the π–π stacking framework are air- and moisture-stable in the solid state. The synthesized electrocatalysts were air-sprayed onto a gas-diffusion electrode as the working electrode. Cu1 is reported to be highly active toward CO2 reduction producing ethylene.30 Cu2 and Cu3 are also electroactive for eCO2RR but with higher selectivity toward multi-carbon products within the same potential range than Cu1 (Figure 1c,d). Figure 1c displays the C1 product profile of 3 electrocatalysts under alkaline eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE. Specifically, CH4 is the dominant product for Cu1, while Cu2 and Cu3 produce ethylene and ethanol as major products (Figure 1d). These results indicate that the structural features of Cu2 and Cu3 preferentially promote the C2 + dominant reaction pathway relative to C1. Although the structurally equivalent CuBtz30 catalyst was previously reported to exhibit high C2 + selectivity, Cu1 displays a C1-dominant product distribution under the conditions employed here. The two studies employed substantially different catalyst-layer configurations, which can alter the local reaction environment and thereby influence the working-state structure and product selectivity of Cu catalysts,42,43 as discussed in Note S1. This contrast further underscores that catalytic behavior cannot be inferred solely from the nominal pristine structure and highlights the importance of correlating product selectivity with the active-state structure observed under operating conditions. Figure 1e compares the partial current density for the C2 + product of 3 electrocatalysts. Cu3 possessed the highest partial current density peaking at –1.2 V vs. RHE, followed by Cu2 and Cu1. However, the ratio of multicarbon products over single carbon products is different among 3 electrocatalysts. We proceed to reveal the structural properties that might lead to the difference in selectivity. Characterization with powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Figure S1) confirmed that the structure is similar to that in previous work30 for Cu1. The XRD pattern of Cu2 shows diffraction features similar to those of Cu1. Compared with the PXRD pattern of Cu1, Cu3 exhibits shifts in several diffraction peaks, suggesting differences in the long-range crystallographic order. Because PXRD alone cannot establish whether the local Cu coordination motif is preserved, the local electronic and coordination structures were further examined later using X-ray absorption spectroscopy. The morphologies of the pristine Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 samples were examined by HR-SEM (Figure S2). Although these morphological differences may affect the electrochemically accessible surface area, product selectivity does not necessarily scale directly with the total accessible surface area. Therefore, the discussion below focuses primarily on the relationship between the distinct local coordination motifs identified and the observed selectivity trends, while recognizing that a contribution from particle morphology cannot be completely excluded. The Raman spectra of the pristine structures confirm the preservation of the triazole ligands after synthesis44 (Figure S3). N K-edge XANES spectra of Cu1 to Cu3 (Figure S4) exhibit nearly identical π* and σ* adsorption features, with no measurable shift in edge onset or variation in the peak position within experimental resolution (0.1 eV). Because N K-edge XAS is sensitive to unoccupied N 2pderived states that reflect metal–ligand orbital mixing and covalency,45 the preserved spectral features indicate comparable Cu–N electronic interactions across all three catalysts, excluding the modulation of the electronic structure as the origin of the divergent product distribution. Cu L-edge spectra display nearly identical white-line intensities and multiplet features for all catalysts (Figure S5), indicating comparable 2p– 3d transition and similar populations of the unoccupied Cu 3d state.46 The preserved spectral features are consistent with a predominantly Cu(I) electronic configuration in the pristine structures. No discernible shift in the L3 edge position is observed, further supporting electronic similarity among the three catalysts. Operando Raman spectroscopy was further employed to probe the interfacial behavior of adsorbed intermediates during eCO2RR (Figure 2). For Cu1, the bands at ∼2050 and 2080 cm–1 are assigned to the low- and high-frequency C≡O stretching modes of linearly adsorbed CO (*CO) on Cu, respectively, consistent with previous in situ and operando vibrational spectroscopic studies.37,47–49 The precise surface environments responsible for these bands may depend on the Cu surface structure, applied potential, and CO coverage. Accordingly, the observed frequency difference may reflect variations in the local Cu–CO coordination environment and Cuto-CO back-donation strength.50 In addition, operando Raman measurements have simultaneously distinguished surfaceadsorbed carbonate at approximately 1055 cm–1 from adsorbed CO at approximately 2080 cm–1, further supporting the assignment of the bands in the 2050–2080 cm–1 region to adsorbed CO rather than carbonate species.51,52 Accordingly, as shown in Figure 2a, the intensity of the *CO2080 band becomes more prominent at more cathodic potential at –1.2 V. Upon reversing the potential sweep, the *CO2050 band is dominant again. Finally, the *CO settled at 2070 cm–1 when back to –0.7 V. The persistence of the *CO signal during the reverse sweep indicates that an appreciable population of surface-bound *CO remains under these conditions, suggesting a relatively stable Cu–*CO interaction and/or slow interfacial CO removal.37 The persistent accumulation of surface-bound *CO may favor subsequent hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products over efficient *CO–*CO coupling. Despite the similar geometric and electronic structures of the three catalysts, the *CO adsorption behavior on Cu2 and Cu3 differs markedly from that on Cu1 (Figure 2b,c). When cathodic potential increases, the *CO in Cu2 shows up at –1.0 V in the range of 2020–2080 cm–1 (Figure 2b). Such substantial spectral broadening implies a heterogeneous and dynamically fluctuating interfacial environment, where *CO experiences a continuum of Cu binding geometries and interaction strengths.37,53,54 When the driving potential further increases to –1.2 V and comes back to –1.1 V vs RHE, the Figure 2. Given the highly dynamic nature of electrocatalytic interfaces under applied potentials,59,61 operando XAS was further employed to probe the evolution of the local electronic and coordination structures of the Cu sites under reaction conditions. The operando XANES remains the same for Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 throughout the applied potentials with no resolvable shifts in the edge fingerprint within the experimental resolution (Figure S7). The observation indicates that the predominantly Cu(I) oxidation state is preserved under the applied potential, which has been proposed to favor *CO–*CO coupling.62 Within the sensitivity of the present measurements, no substantial ensemble-averaged electronic restructuring is detected. Subtle charge redistribution, adsorbate-induced changes in metal–ligand covalency, transient electronic states, or changes confined to a minority population of the active site may not be resolved by XANES. Accordingly, Cu–Cu geometry evolution represents the dominant changes detected under the relevant operando conditions. Figure 3c–e shows the evolution of coordination shells for Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3, respectively, during alkaline CO2 electroreduction. From Figure 3c, Fourier-transform EXAFS spectra (k3-weighted, 2.5 to 10.5 Å–1) reveal progressive splitting of the Cu–Cu scattering feature centered at ∼3.5 Å under increasing cathodic bias from –0.7 to –0.9 V. This evolution indicates the emergence of asymmetric Cu– Cu coordination. Further EXAFS fitting yields a contraction of one Cu–Cu distance from 3.68 ± 0.02 to 3.54 ± 0.01 Å, accompanied by expansion of a second path to 4.05 ± 0.01 Å from –0.7 to –1.2 V vs RHE. The prominent peak of Cu–N2 also shows distortion alongside, in resonance to the stretch of the coordination structure around the copper centers, which supports the suspected asymmetric Cu–Cu spacing. Conversely, the Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 remains unchanged at all cathodic potentials, as shown in Figure 3d,e, respectively. WT-EXAFS is particularly useful when different scattering paths appear at a similar apparent radial distance in Fourier-transform EXAFS because it provides simultaneous resolution in both R-space and k-space.64,65 Since the backscattering amplitude depends strongly on the atomic number of the scatterer, heavier atoms generally give stronger contributions at higher k values. Therefore, WT-EXAFS can help distinguish Cu scatterers from lighter C/N scatterers based on their different k-space intensity distribution.66 The WT-EXAFS contour plot of pristine Cu1 (Figure 4a) shows three major lobes assigned to Cu–N1, Cu–N2, and Cu– Cu scattering paths. These features appear at apparent distances of ∼1.7, 2.5, and 3.5 Å, with k-space maxima centered near 4.5, 4.5, and 6.5 Å–1, respectively. Under cathodic bias at –1.2 V vs RHE (Figure 4b), the Cu–Cu scattering feature broadens and shifts relative to the pristine state. Enlarged views of the Cu– Cu region (Figure 4c,d) reveal the emergence of additional high-k contribution centered near 8 Å–1 at an apparent distance of ∼3.2 Å, together with an expanded Cu–Cu feature extended toward ∼3.8 Å with a k-space maximum near 6.5 Å–1. These results therefore corroborate the operando FT-EXAFS observation that Cu1 undergoes asymmetric Cu– Cu distortion under cathodic bias. Time-dependent operando XAS further confirms that Cu1 retains a distorted local coordination framework without complete collapse during 3 h of continuous eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE (Figure S32). We propose that the ligand-derived steric confinement (Figure 5) stabilizes the Cu–Cu configuration in Cu2 and Cu3 by restricting Cu-site displacement and suppressing pronounced asymmetric distortion. This structural persistence could preserve the integrity of their local coordination environments under applied bias, thereby maintaining welldefined sites for the adsorption and conversion of eCO2RR intermediates. Specifically, the onset potential of Cu–Cu splitting at –0.9 V corresponds to the onset potential when two distinct *CO bands (2050 and 2080 cm–1) emerged with Cu1. The shortened Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuS) may induce stronger confinement of adsorbed *CO species, potentially altering their adsorption configuration from terminal-like to more bridge-like coordination. In contrast, the elongated Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuL) likely increases the separation between neighboring adsorbates, thereby reducing the probability of effective *CO–*CO coupling. Such asymmetric Cu–Cu environments may therefore favor sequential hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products, consistent with the enhanced CH4 selectivity observed for Cu1 in Figure 1c. In contrast, the preserved Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 under cathodic bias may better maintain favorable geometric configurations for *CO–*CO coupling. Accordingly, the preservation of symmetric Cu–Cu spacing provides a stable geometric environment favorable for sustained C–C coupling. The introduction of steric hindrance through ligand modification on either benzoic ring or azole nitrogen therefore plays a critical role in preserving the intrinsic Cu–Cu spacing as it is under bias. The absence of detectable changes in the electronic structure of copper under bias further supports the conclusion that geometric stability, rather than electronic modulation, governs the divergent reaction pathways. With that being said, localized rearrangements cannot be completely excluded. Local interfacial electric fields may also influence C–C coupling by stabilizing polar intermediates such as *OCCO through field–dipole interactions.70,71 Taken together, these results establish Cu–Cu geometric persistence as the dominant structural descriptor governing C2 + selectivity in this catalyst series, while other potential microenvironmental factors arising at the catalyst–electrolyte interface may also contribute. The performance of Cu1–Cu3 was compared with that of representative molecular Cu-based catalysts containing adjacent Cu sites (Table S4). Cu2 and Cu3 exhibit C2 + performance within the reported range; however, no simple relationship between Cu–Cu distance and C2 + selectivity is evident. Notably, operando Cu–Cu structures are unavailable for most reported catalysts, limiting direct structure–activity comparisons. To sum up, these findings highlight the necessity of operando characterization to capture the dynamic structural evolution under bias, even for catalysts with structurally welldefined molecular motifs that appear preserved after catalysis by ex situ characterization. ■CONCLUSIONS This work demonstrates that the divergent catalytic behaviors of dual-Cu-site catalysts originate from their distinct active-state structural evolution under reaction conditions rather than differences in their initial coordination structures or electronic states. Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that Cu1 undergoes asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, resulting in heterogeneous *CO binding environments that favor C1 pathways, whereas the sterically stabilized Cu2 and Cu3 preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain C–C coupling toward enhanced C2 + formation. These findings establish geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions as a critical parameter for multicarbon CO2 electroreduction.

evidence.quote: Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that catalysts with insufficient steric constraint undergo asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, leading to heterogeneous *CO adsorption behavior and enhanced C1 pathways. In contrast, sterically stabilized catalysts preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain favorable *CO–*CO coupling toward C2 + formation. These findings demonstrate that geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions, rather than the initial structure alone, governs catalytic selectivity in CO2 electroreduction and highlights the importance of operando characterization for identifying active-state structures. KEYWORDS: eCO2RR, secondary coordination sphere, local environment, operando spectroscopy, Cu–Cu distance ■INTRODUCTION Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) offers a promising strategy for converting CO2 into value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable electricity.1–3 Although recent advances in electrolyzer engineering have enabled CO2RR at industrially relevant current density and selectivity,4,5 achieving highly selective multi-carbon (C2 +) production remains a major challenge due to the complex reaction pathways involved in C–C coupling6 and the associated separation cost of mixed products.7,8 The formation of multi-carbon products during eCO2RR involves complex proton-coupled multi-electron transfer pathways and kinetically demanding C–C coupling processes, often resulting in broad product distributions and reduced selectivity.9,10 Consequently, catalyst design strategies capable of regulating intermediate adsorption and coupling behavior are critically important for improving multi-carbon selectivity.11,12 In ligand-coordinated Cu catalysts, the formation of multicarbon products has been strongly associated with the presence of adjacent Cu centers.13,14 Cu is uniquely capable among monometallic catalysts of producing substantial multi-carbon products by eCO2RR.3,15 However, isolated Cu single sites predominantly produce single-carbon products under reaction conditions,16–20 whereas paired Cu centers have been associated with enhanced C2 + formation.21 Previous studies further revealed that replacing one Cu center with heteroatoms significantly alters intermediate adsorption energetics and suppresses multi-carbon pathways,22 suggesting that adjacent Cu centers play a critical role in C–C coupling during eCO2RR. Motivated by this mechanistic hypothesis, increasing efforts have focused on engineering the microenvironment of the Cu active site,23–25 especially the Cu–Cu spacing in multinuclear Cu catalysts. Recent studies have reported dual- and multinuclear Cu systems with Cu–Cu distances ranging from 2.54 to 3.52 Å, including halogen-bridged dual-copper catalysts,14,26,27 carbon supported molecular catalysts,28 metal–organic polymers,29 and triazole-bridged MOF structures,30 all demonstrating appreciable C2 + selectivity under eCO2RR conditions. The importance of Cu–Cu spacing has been attributed to its influence on the adsorption geometry and coupling probability of adjacent *CO intermediates, which are widely considered key steps toward multi-carbon formation.10,31,32 Accordingly, considerable efforts have been devoted to rigidly controlling Received: June 4, 2026 Revised: August 7, 2026 Accepted: August 7, 2026 www.acsami.org Research Article This article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.6c11350 ACS Appl. Despite the growing emphasis on Cu–Cu spacing engineering, the structural evolution of dual-Cu sites under operating conditions remains poorly understood. Previous studies have provided valuable structural insights through pre- and postreaction characterization; however, direct operando observations of Cu–Cu dynamics during eCO2RR remain scarce. (Figure 1a) Given the highly dynamic nature of electrocatalytic interfaces under bias,33,34 static structural assignments obtained before or after reaction may not fully capture the realistic catalytic configurations responsible for intermediate coupling during eCO2RR. Such configurational flexibility has been proposed to provide diverse adsorption geometries for adjacent *CO intermediates, potentially facilitating C–C coupling toward multi-carbon products.26,35 However, without direct experimental evidence confirming reversible Cu–Cu stretching under reaction conditions, its relationship to catalytic selectivity has yet to be experimentally established. Here, we investigate how ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution and selectivity of a series of trinuclear Cu catalysts during eCO2RR. By combining operando X-ray absorption and Raman spectroscopies,36,37 we track changes in Cu–Cu coordination and *CO adsorption under working conditions. We find that catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu–Cu configuration and favor C2 + formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity. These results identify active-state geometric persistence, rather than the initial coordination structure alone, as a key design parameter for eCO2RR targeting multi-carbon products.36,37 ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Materials All reagents and chemicals were commercially available and used without further purification. The synthesized electrocatalysts were air-sprayed onto a gas-diffusion electrode as the working electrode. Cu1 is reported to be highly active toward CO2 reduction producing ethylene.30 Cu2 and Cu3 are also electroactive for eCO2RR but with higher selectivity toward multi-carbon products within the same potential range than Cu1 (Figure 1c,d). Figure 1c displays the C1 product profile of 3 electrocatalysts under alkaline eCO2RR at –1.2 V vs RHE. Specifically, CH4 is the dominant product for Cu1, while Cu2 and Cu3 produce ethylene and ethanol as major products (Figure 1d). These results indicate that the structural features of Cu2 and Cu3 preferentially promote the C2 + dominant reaction pathway relative to C1. Although the structurally equivalent CuBtz30 catalyst was previously reported to exhibit high C2 + selectivity, Cu1 displays a C1-dominant product distribution under the conditions employed here. The two studies employed substantially different catalyst-layer configurations, which can alter the local reaction environment and thereby influence the working-state structure and product selectivity of Cu catalysts,42,43 as discussed in Note S1. This contrast further underscores that catalytic behavior cannot be inferred solely from the nominal pristine structure and highlights the importance of correlating product selectivity with the active-state structure observed under operating conditions. Figure 1e compares the partial current density for the C2 + product of 3 electrocatalysts. Cu3 possessed the highest partial current density peaking at –1.2 V vs. RHE, followed by Cu2 and Cu1. However, the ratio of multicarbon products over single carbon products is different among 3 electrocatalysts. Characterization with powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Figure S1) confirmed that the structure is similar to that in previous work30 for Cu1. Because PXRD alone cannot establish whether the local Cu coordination motif is preserved, the local electronic and coordination structures were further examined later using X-ray absorption spectroscopy. The morphologies of the pristine Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 samples were examined by HR-SEM (Figure S2). Although these morphological differences may affect the electrochemically accessible surface area, product selectivity does not necessarily scale directly with the total accessible surface area. Therefore, the discussion below focuses primarily on the relationship between the distinct local coordination motifs identified and the observed selectivity trends, while recognizing that a contribution from particle morphology cannot be completely excluded. The Raman spectra of the pristine structures confirm the preservation of the triazole ligands after synthesis44 (Figure S3). N K-edge XANES spectra of Cu1 to Cu3 (Figure S4) exhibit nearly identical π* and σ* adsorption features, with no measurable shift in edge onset or variation in the peak position within experimental resolution (0.1 eV). Because N K-edge XAS is sensitive to unoccupied N 2pderived states that reflect metal–ligand orbital mixing and covalency,45 the preserved spectral features indicate comparable Cu–N electronic interactions across all three catalysts, excluding the modulation of the electronic structure as the origin of the divergent product distribution. Cu L-edge spectra display nearly identical white-line intensities and multiplet features for all catalysts (Figure S5), indicating comparable 2p– 3d transition and similar populations of the unoccupied Cu 3d state.46 The preserved spectral features are consistent with a predominantly Cu(I) electronic configuration in the pristine structures. No discernible shift in the L3 edge position is observed, further supporting electronic similarity among the three catalysts. Operando Raman spectroscopy was further employed to probe the interfacial behavior of adsorbed intermediates during eCO2RR (Figure 2). For Cu1, the bands at ∼2050 and 2080 cm–1 are assigned to the low- and high-frequency C≡O stretching modes of linearly adsorbed CO (*CO) on Cu, respectively, consistent with previous in situ and operando vibrational spectroscopic studies.37,47–49 The precise surface environments responsible for these bands may depend on the Cu surface structure, applied potential, and CO coverage. Accordingly, the observed frequency difference may reflect variations in the local Cu–CO coordination environment and Cuto-CO back-donation strength.50 In addition, operando Raman measurements have simultaneously distinguished surfaceadsorbed carbonate at approximately 1055 cm–1 from adsorbed CO at approximately 2080 cm–1, further supporting the assignment of the bands in the 2050–2080 cm–1 region to adsorbed CO rather than carbonate species.51,52 Accordingly, as shown in Figure 2a, the intensity of the *CO2080 band becomes more prominent at more cathodic potential at –1.2 V. Upon reversing the potential sweep, the *CO2050 band is dominant again. Finally, the *CO settled at 2070 cm–1 when back to –0.7 V. The persistence of the *CO signal during the reverse sweep indicates that an appreciable population of surface-bound *CO remains under these conditions, suggesting a relatively stable Cu–*CO interaction and/or slow interfacial CO removal.37 The persistent accumulation of surface-bound *CO may favor subsequent hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products over efficient *CO–*CO coupling. Despite the similar geometric and electronic structures of the three catalysts, the *CO adsorption behavior on Cu2 and Cu3 differs markedly from that on Cu1 (Figure 2b,c). When cathodic potential increases, the *CO in Cu2 shows up at –1.0 V in the range of 2020–2080 cm–1 (Figure 2b). We propose that the ligand-derived steric confinement (Figure 5) stabilizes the Cu–Cu configuration in Cu2 and Cu3 by restricting Cu-site displacement and suppressing pronounced asymmetric distortion. This structural persistence could preserve the integrity of their local coordination environments under applied bias, thereby maintaining welldefined sites for the adsorption and conversion of eCO2RR intermediates. Specifically, the onset potential of Cu–Cu splitting at –0.9 V corresponds to the onset potential when two distinct *CO bands (2050 and 2080 cm–1) emerged with Cu1. The shortened Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuS) may induce stronger confinement of adsorbed *CO species, potentially altering their adsorption configuration from terminal-like to more bridge-like coordination. In contrast, the elongated Cu–Cu spacing (Cu–CuL) likely increases the separation between neighboring adsorbates, thereby reducing the probability of effective *CO–*CO coupling. Such asymmetric Cu–Cu environments may therefore favor sequential hydrogenation pathways toward C1 products, consistent with the enhanced CH4 selectivity observed for Cu1 in Figure 1c. In contrast, the preserved Cu–Cu spacing in Cu2 and Cu3 under cathodic bias may better maintain favorable geometric configurations for *CO–*CO coupling. Accordingly, the preservation of symmetric Cu–Cu spacing provides a stable geometric environment favorable for sustained C–C coupling. The introduction of steric hindrance through ligand modification on either benzoic ring or azole nitrogen therefore plays a critical role in preserving the intrinsic Cu–Cu spacing as it is under bias. The absence of detectable changes in the electronic structure of copper under bias further supports the conclusion that geometric stability, rather than electronic modulation, governs the divergent reaction pathways. With that being said, localized rearrangements cannot be completely excluded. Local interfacial electric fields may also influence C–C coupling by stabilizing polar intermediates such as *OCCO through field–dipole interactions.70,71 Taken together, these results establish Cu–Cu geometric persistence as the dominant structural descriptor governing C2 + selectivity in this catalyst series, while other potential microenvironmental factors arising at the catalyst–electrolyte interface may also contribute. The performance of Cu1–Cu3 was compared with that of representative molecular Cu-based catalysts containing adjacent Cu sites (Table S4). Cu2 and Cu3 exhibit C2 + performance within the reported range; however, no simple relationship between Cu–Cu distance and C2 + selectivity is evident. Notably, operando Cu–Cu structures are unavailable for most reported catalysts, limiting direct structure–activity comparisons. To sum up, these findings highlight the necessity of operando characterization to capture the dynamic structural evolution under bias, even for catalysts with structurally welldefined molecular motifs that appear preserved after catalysis by ex situ characterization. ■CONCLUSIONS This work demonstrates that the divergent catalytic behaviors of dual-Cu-site catalysts originate from their distinct active-state structural evolution under reaction conditions rather than differences in their initial coordination structures or electronic states. Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that Cu1 undergoes asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, resulting in heterogeneous *CO binding environments that favor C1 pathways, whereas the sterically stabilized Cu2 and Cu3 preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain C–C coupling toward enhanced C2 + formation. These findings establish geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions as a critical parameter for multicarbon CO2 electroreduction.

Operando Raman and X-ray absorption spectroscopies reveal that catalysts with insufficient steric constraint undergo asymmetric Cu–Cu distortion under cathodic bias, leading to heterogeneous *CO adsorption behavior and enhanced C1 pathways. In contrast, sterically stabilized catalysts preserve symmetric Cu–Cu configurations and sustain favorable *CO–*CO coupling toward C2 + formation. These findings demonstrate that geometric persistence of neighboring Cu sites under operating conditions, rather than the initial structure alone, governs catalytic selectivity in CO2 electroreduction and highlights the importance of operando characterization for identifying active-state structures. KEYWORDS: eCO2RR, secondary coordination sphere, local environment, operando spectroscopy, Cu–Cu distance ■INTRODUCTION Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) offers a promising strategy for converting CO2 into value-added chemicals and fuels using renewable electricity.1–3 Although recent advances in electrolyzer engineering have enabled CO2RR at industrially relevant current density and selectivity,4,5 achieving highly selective multi-carbon (C2 +) production remains a major challenge due to the complex reaction pathways involved in C–C coupling6 and the associated separation cost of mixed products.7,8 The formation of multi-carbon products during eCO2RR involves complex proton-coupled multi-electron transfer pathways and kinetically demanding C–C coupling processes, often resulting in broad product distributions and reduced selectivity.9,10 Consequently, catalyst design strategies capable of regulating intermediate adsorption and coupling behavior are critically important for improving multi-carbon selectivity.11,12 In ligand-coordinated Cu catalysts, the formation of multicarbon products has been strongly associated with the presence of adjacent Cu centers.13,14 Cu is uniquely capable among monometallic catalysts of producing substantial multi-carbon products by eCO2RR.3,15 However, isolated Cu single sites predominantly produce single-carbon products under reaction conditions,16–20 whereas paired Cu centers have been associated with enhanced C2 + formation.21 Previous studies further revealed that replacing one Cu center with heteroatoms significantly alters intermediate adsorption energetics and suppresses multi-carbon pathways,22 suggesting that adjacent Cu centers play a critical role in C–C coupling during eCO2RR. Motivated by this mechanistic hypothesis, increasing efforts have focused on engineering the microenvironment of the Cu active site,23–25 especially the Cu–Cu spacing in multinuclear Cu catalysts. Recent studies have reported dual- and multinuclear Cu systems with Cu–Cu distances ranging from 2.54 to 3.52 Å, including halogen-bridged dual-copper catalysts,14,26,27 carbon supported molecular catalysts,28 metal–organic polymers,29 and triazole-bridged MOF structures,30 all demonstrating appreciable C2 + selectivity under eCO2RR conditions. Despite the growing emphasis on Cu–Cu spacing engineering, the structural evolution of dual-Cu sites under operating conditions remains poorly understood. Previous studies have provided valuable structural insights through pre- and postreaction characterization; however, direct operando observations of Cu–Cu dynamics during eCO2RR remain scarce. (Figure 1a) Given the highly dynamic nature of electrocatalytic interfaces under bias,33,34 static structural assignments obtained before or after reaction may not fully capture the realistic catalytic configurations responsible for intermediate coupling during eCO2RR. Such configurational flexibility has been proposed to provide diverse adsorption geometries for adjacent *CO intermediates, potentially facilitating C–C coupling toward multi-carbon products.26,35 However, without direct experimental evidence confirming reversible Cu–Cu stretching under reaction conditions, its relationship to catalytic selectivity has yet to be experimentally established. Here, we investigate how ligand-imposed structural rigidity governs the active-state evolution and selectivity of a series of trinuclear Cu catalysts during eCO2RR. By combining operando X-ray absorption and Raman spectroscopies,36,37 we track changes in Cu–Cu coordination and *CO adsorption under working conditions. We find that catalysts with greater steric rigidity better preserve their Cu–Cu configuration and favor C2 + formation, whereas structurally flexible motifs undergo distortion and show increased C1 selectivity. These results identify active-state geometric persistence, rather than the initial coordination structure alone, as a key design parameter for eCO2RR targeting multi-carbon products.36,37 ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Materials All reagents and chemicals were commercially available and used without further purification.
